verdict.reasoning: Patient reports soreness and cracked skin of hands, mainly palms, for 'a couple of months... three, four months ago' and notes 'it's itchy... it does get itchy' and 'it hurts a lot.'
Doctor asks if she came because it has worsened; patient answers 'Yeah I mean, it's gotten to a point where, where it hurts a lot. And I can't really do my job.'
In social history, doctor asks about work impact; patient says 'yeah like the past three days, I haven't been able to go to work.'

She reports 'soreness in my fingers... the skin on my hands is kind of cracked,' confirms 'the palm' is affected and that 'it's itchy. Not all the time, but yeah, it does get itchy,' consistent with palmar dryness, fissuring, and intermittent pruritus.
On bleeding: patient says 'no I don't think so' then clarifies 'yeah I guess when I scratched it, yes it has bled sometimes but... it hasn't bled on its own.'
She notes 'I have dryness, like you know, in other parts, like my legs. But it's not... very severe' and 'I've always, you know, I don't hydrate very much.'
Past medical history: Patient says 'I have diabetes.' Doctor asks 'type one or type two?' Patient replies 'Type two.'
When asked about medications, the transcript shows 'Doctor: Metformin, OK.' indicating metformin use.
She states 'Yeah. I tried uh E forty five.' and later 'Yeah, no it didn't really do anything.' indicating OTC E45 emollient with no benefit.
Patient says 'I also tried an antihistamine, antihistamine. Uh but it didn't—' and doctor responds, indicating an OTC antihistamine was tried without benefit.
Doctor asks 'Do you have any allergies, either to any medications or in general?' Patient replies 'No.'
Patient states 'I do work as a housekeeper' and later clarifies 'At a hotel. I have to do the whole thing like bedrooms, bathrooms.'
Social history: 'Do you smoke at all?' Patient: 'No.' Regarding alcohol, patient reports 'a couple of pints a week,' and doctor summarizes 'very minimal, alcohol there.'
Family history: Doctor says 'Family history-wise, is there anything I should be aware of? ... Diabetes as well.' indicating family history of diabetes.
Doctor asks about 'fever, or temperatures', 'nausea, or any vomiting', 'problem with your bowels?', 'problem with your urine, or waterworks?' Patient answers 'No' to each.
Doctor asks if she 'otherwise you feel well' and about 'eating, drinking, your appetite'; patient responds 'Yeah.'

Doctor states 'I think you might have something called dermatitis or contact dermatitis... particularly people... using cleaning products, not using gloves. And sometimes you get a bit of reaction between the chemicals and your skin,' consistent with irritant contact dermatitis related to cleaning products of the palms.
The condition description matches earlier symptoms: dryness/xerosis and cracking/fissuring ('skin on my hands is kind of cracked') with 'it's itchy... it does get itchy,' i.e., intermittent pruritus.
Patient notes it 'hurts a lot. And I can't really do my job,' and later confirms being off work three days, showing pain and work limitation.
Management: 'what we try and do is, you know, avoid the triggers. In your case, I strongly recommend that you wear gloves when cleaning at all times.'
Doctor says 'we can try some steroid creams to help with the inflammation,' referring to treatment of the affected hands/palms.
Doctor plans 'some stronger emollients, um which you really need to kind of coat on, three four times a day, for the next couple of weeks,' consistent with 3–4 times daily for about 10–14 days.
When asked where to get the medicine, doctor replies 'I'll... do a prescription for you now, and send it over to your pharmacy,' indicating an electronic prescription.

Doctor advises 'if it still hasn't got better in about a week, two weeks time, I really need you to come back and see me again' and also 'if it's spreading, or dryness is getting worse, come back and see me sooner.'

'If it still hasn't got better in about a week, two weeks time, I really need you to come back... And we can maybe think about other things we can give to you,' implying reassessment and considering alternative/adjunct treatments.

She works as a hotel housekeeper, not always good at wearing gloves, and uses products especially for bathrooms: 'I usually use those for bathrooms. But, yeah bedrooms and corridors not always' with doctor linking chemicals to symptoms.
Patient says 'I switched jobs, uh four months ago' and earlier notes symptoms started 'a couple of months ago... three, four months ago,' indicating a job change about four months prior.
